experienceLevelMapping.note: App convention mapping the profile's 1-10 self-assessment onto the literature's novice/intermediate/advanced categories. The mapping itself is not evidence-based. Where a source distinguishes 'trained' vs 'untrained' populations, untrained is mapped to novice and trained to intermediate/advanced.

value.unit: sets per muscle group per week

variables.recommendation: Perform at least 10 weekly sets per muscle group to maximize muscle growth. Lower volumes (<=4 weekly sets) still produce substantial (smaller) gains and are a valid starting point.
variables.finding: Graded dose-response: <5, 5-9, and 10+ weekly sets produced 5.4%, 6.6%, and 9.8% muscle growth respectively; each additional weekly set added ~0.37% gain. Authors: 'performance of at least 10 weekly sets per muscle group is necessary to maximise increases in muscle mass.'
caveats: Upper limit unknown: 'the paucity of data investigating weekly volumes of >12 sets prevented analysis of very high training volumes' - do not extrapolate far beyond ~10-12 sets from this source alone.
Evidence base is mostly untrained individuals; only two included studies used resistance-trained subjects.
Authors advise monitoring individual response and adjusting dosage rather than applying the number rigidly.

value.unit: sessions per muscle group per week

variables.recommendation: Choose weekly training frequency per muscle group by preference and practicality; what matters is accumulating the weekly set target. Spreading volume over 2+ sessions per muscle is a reasonable default and was superior in earlier evidence.
variables.finding: 2016 meta-analysis: training a muscle 2x/week outperformed 1x/week (6.8% vs 3.7% growth) on a volume-equated basis. The larger 2019 follow-up (25 studies) revised this: 'resistance training frequency does not significantly or meaningfully impact muscle hypertrophy when volume is equated. Thus, for a given training volume, individuals can choose a weekly frequency per muscle groups based on personal preference.'
caveats: The two meta-analyses disagree; the 2019 (larger, newer) conclusion is treated as operative here.
Whether >3 sessions per muscle per week helps or harms is unstudied in the included literature.

variables.recommendation: Rest more than 2 minutes between sets to maximize strength gains in resistance-trained individuals.
variables.finding: 'It seems that longer duration RIs (>2 min) are required to maximize strength gains in resistance-trained individuals.' (23 studies, 491 participants)
caveats: Trained/untrained population split mapped onto intermediate-advanced/novice per the experienceLevelMapping note.
Extracted from abstract; full text was paywalled.

variables.recommendation: Rest 60-120 seconds between sets; in untrained individuals this is sufficient to maximize strength gains.
variables.finding: 'With regard to untrained individuals, it seems that short to moderate RIs (60-120 s) are sufficient for maximizing muscular strength gains.'
caveats: Trained/untrained population split mapped onto intermediate-advanced/novice per the experienceLevelMapping note.
Extracted from abstract; full text was paywalled.

variables.recommendation: Both short (<=60 s) and long (>60 s) rest intervals can produce hypertrophy; for trained individuals, evidence suggests a possible advantage for long (>60 s) rest intervals.
variables.finding: 'Both short and long inter-set rest intervals may be useful when training for achieving gains in muscle hypertrophy. Novel findings involving trained participants using measures sensitive to detect changes in muscle hypertrophy suggest a possible advantage for the use of long rest intervals.'
caveats: Only six studies met inclusion; authors call for more research before a clear differentiation.
'Long' is defined in the source only as >60 seconds - no specific upper prescription is given.
Extracted from abstract; full text was paywalled.

variables.recommendation: Terminate most sets close to failure, but reaching outright momentary muscular failure is not required. If sets are taken to failure, bias that toward low-complexity exercises (e.g. single-joint), the last set of an exercise, and lower per-session set volumes, to limit accumulated fatigue.
variables.finding: Hypertrophy increases as sets are terminated closer to failure (negative dose-response slopes in all best-fit meta-regression models), but momentary failure showed no advantage over non-failure (ES 0.12, p=0.343). The verified literature quantifies direction only - it does NOT prescribe a numeric RIR range; any specific '0-2 RIR' style number is practitioner interpretation, not a sourced finding.
caveats: No verified numeric RIR target exists - treat 'close to failure' qualitatively.
Robinson et al. call their analysis exploratory and warn the exact RIR relationship remains unclear.
Robinson et al. extracted from abstract; full text was paywalled.

variables.recommendation: Proximity to failure does not meaningfully drive strength gains - strength improves similarly across a wide range of reps-in-reserve. Do not sacrifice load or technique to chase failure when strength is the goal.
variables.finding: 'Strength gains were similar across a wide range of RIR, while muscle hypertrophy improves as sets are terminated closer to failure.' (all best-fit strength models had marginal RIR slopes whose confidence intervals contained the null)
caveats: Extracted from abstract; full text was paywalled.
Authors describe the analysis as exploratory.

variables.recommendation: Order exercises by priority: put the exercises most important to the user's goal first in the session, regardless of muscle size or compound/isolation status. Blanket 'compound before isolation' is NOT what the evidence says.
variables.finding: Strength gains are largest for exercises performed first in a session (Nunes 2021: MJ-first favors MJ strength ES 0.32, SJ-first favors SJ strength ES -0.58), while exercise order has no significant effect on hypertrophy (ES 0.03, p=0.862). Simao 2012: 'exercises be ordered based on priority of importance as dictated by the training goal of a programme, irrespective of whether the exercise involves a relatively large or small muscle group.'
caveats: Simao and Nunes extracted from abstracts; full texts were paywalled.
Total-session volume is higher for whatever is placed early - placement is a prioritization tool.

The older ACSM position stand (2009) recommends large-before-small / multi-joint-before-single-joint sequencing; the newer meta-analytic evidence above supersedes it for hypertrophy (order has no effect) and reframes it for strength (whatever goes first improves most).

variables.recommendation: Train with loads of roughly 60-70% of 1RM for 8-12 repetitions per set.
variables.finding: 'Training with loads ~60-70% of 1 RM for 8-12 repetitions for novice to intermediate individuals' (Evidence Category A).
caveats: The document gives one approximate range for novice-to-intermediate; it does not separate the two levels for strength loading.

variables.recommendation: Cycle loads of 80-100% of 1RM in a periodized manner.
variables.finding: 'cycling loads of 80-100% of 1 RM for advanced individuals' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Increase the load by 2-10% when the current workload can be performed for 1-2 repetitions over the target on two consecutive sessions.
variables.finding: 'a 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for 1-2 repetitions over the desired number on two consecutive training sessions' (Evidence Category B).

variables.recommendation: Use 1-3 sets per exercise as a novice.
variables.finding: 'It is recommended that 1-3 sets per exercise be used by novice individuals' (Evidence Category A). For intermediate/advanced progression the document recommends multiple-set programs with systematic variation of volume and intensity, without fixing a number.

variables.recommendation: Train the entire body 2-3 days per week.
variables.finding: 'It is recommended that novice individuals train the entire body 2-3 d/wk' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Train 3-4 days per week.
variables.finding: 'for progression to intermediate training, a frequency of 3-4 d/wk be used' (Evidence Category B).

variables.recommendation: Train 4-6 days per week using muscle-group or upper/lower splits.
variables.finding: 'It is recommended that advanced lifters train 4-6 d/wk' (Evidence Category C, Table 2).
caveats: Internal inconsistency in the source: the abstract says 4-5 d/wk for advanced training while Table 2 says 4-6 d/wk. Both appear in the published document.

variables.recommendation: Rest at least 2-3 minutes between sets of core (heavy, multi-joint) exercises at all experience levels; 1-2 minutes may suffice for assistance exercises.
variables.finding: 'It is recommended that rest periods of at least 2-3 min be used for core exercises using heavier loads for novice, intermediate, and advanced training. For assistance exercises, a shorter rest period length of 1-2 min may suffice.' (Evidence Categories B/C)
caveats: Consistent with the meta-analytic rest_between_sets rule (>2 min to maximize strength in trained individuals).

variables.recommendation: Use moderate loading of 70-85% of 1RM for 8-12 repetitions per set, 1-3 sets per exercise.
variables.finding: 'For novice and intermediate training, it is recommended that moderate loading be used (70-85% of 1 RM) for 8-12 repetitions per set for 1-3 sets per exercise' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Use 70-100% of 1RM for 1-12 repetitions per set, 3-6 sets per exercise, periodized so most training sits in the 6-12RM range.
variables.finding: 'For advanced training, it is recommended that a loading range of 70-100% of 1 RM be used for 1-12 repetitions per set for 3-6 sets per exercise in a periodized manner such that the majority of training is devoted to 6-12 RM and less training devoted to 1-6 RM loading' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Rest 1-2 minutes between sets for novice and intermediate hypertrophy training.
variables.finding: 'It is recommended that 1- to 2-min rest periods be used in novice and intermediate training' (Evidence Category C). For advanced training the document ties rest to the exercise's goal: 2-3 min for heavy core lifts, 1-2 min otherwise.
caveats: The newer meta-analytic rest_between_sets rule suggests a possible advantage for longer (>60 s) rest in trained individuals - both entries are served so the client can weigh tiers.

variables.recommendation: Train 2-3 days per week (whole-body sessions).
variables.finding: 'a frequency of 2-3 d/wk be used for novice training' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Train 2-3 days per week for total-body workouts, or 4 days per week using an upper/lower split.
variables.finding: 'For intermediate training, the recommendation is similar for total-body workouts or 4 d/wk when using an upper/lower body split routine' (Evidence Category B).

variables.recommendation: Train 4-6 days per week.
variables.finding: 'For advanced training, a frequency of 4-6 d/wk is recommended' (Evidence Category C).

variables.recommendation: Use light-to-moderate loads (40-60% of 1RM) for high repetitions (>15) with short rest periods (<90 s).
variables.finding: Abstract: 'light to moderate loads (40-60% of 1 RM) be performed for high repetitions (>15) using short rest periods (<90 s)'.

variables.recommendation: Use relatively light loads for 10-15 repetitions with moderate to high volume.
variables.finding: 'For novice and intermediate training, it is recommended that relatively light loads be used (10-15 repetitions) with moderate to high volume' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Use varied loading strategies for multiple sets of 10-25+ repetitions in a periodized manner, with higher overall volume at lighter intensities.
variables.finding: 'For advanced training, it is recommended that various loading strategies be used for multiple sets per exercise (10-25 repetitions or more) in a periodized manner leading to a higher overall volume using lighter intensities' (Evidence Category C).

variables.recommendation: Keep rest short: 1-2 minutes for high-repetition sets (15-20+ reps), under 1 minute for moderate sets (10-15 reps).
variables.finding: 'It is recommended that short rest periods be used for muscular endurance training, e.g., 1-2 min for high-repetition sets (15-20 repetitions or more), less than 1 minute for moderate (10-15 repetitions) sets' (Evidence Category C).

variables.recommendation: Train the entire body 2-3 days per week.
variables.finding: 'Low frequency (2-3 d/wk) is effective in novice individuals when training the entire body' (Evidence Category A).

variables.recommendation: Train 3 days per week for total-body workouts, 4 days per week for an upper/lower split.
variables.finding: 'For intermediate training, 3 d/wk is recommended for total-body workouts and 4 d/wk is recommended for upper/lower body split routine workouts' (Evidence Category C).

variables.recommendation: A higher frequency (4-6 days per week) may be used with muscle-group split routines.
variables.finding: 'For advanced training, a higher frequency may be used (4-6 d/wk) if muscle group split routines are used' (Evidence Category C).

variables.population: older adults (65+ per NSCA definition; 'older than 60' for the intensity figure)
variables.recommendation: For older adults: 2-3 sets of 6-12 repetitions at 50-85% of 1RM per muscle group; in healthy adults over 60, intensity should reach 70-85% of 1RM. Training to outright failure is not necessary - 50-70% of the maximal possible repetitions in good form is sufficient.
variables.finding: '2-3 sets of 6-12 repetitions at 50-85% of 1RM per muscle group should be prescribed to promote greater maximal strength and muscle size gains'; 'in healthy adults older than 60 years of age, resistance training intensity should achieve 70-85% of 1RM'; 'repetitions to failure are not necessary and do not promote additional physiological adaptations in older individuals'.
caveats: Population is 65+/60+. No locatable evidence supports modified prescriptions starting at age 45 - the original design's '45+ modifiers' (joint-friendly variants, mandatory warm-up, RIR cap) were checked and are NOT evidence-backed at that threshold; do not apply this rule to middle-aged users.

variables.population: healthy old adults (studies aged 60+, analyzed cohort mean age 70.4)
variables.recommendation: Doses associated with the largest effects in older adults - strength: 2 sessions/week, 2-3 sets per exercise, 7-9 reps per set, 70-79% of 1RM, 60 s rest between sets. Muscle morphology: 3 sessions/week, 2-3 sets, 7-9 reps, 51-69% of 1RM, 120 s rest between sets.
variables.finding: For strength: 'a training intensity of 70-79% of the one-repetition maximum (1RM)... a rest in between sets of 60 s... a training frequency of two sessions per week, a training volume of two to three sets per exercise, seven to nine repetitions per set'. For morphology: 'a training frequency of three sessions per week... a training intensity from 51 to 69% of the 1RM... a rest of 120 s between sets'.
caveats: Derived from studies with mean cohort age 70.4 - not evidence for younger users.
The associated training periods in the source were ~50-53 weeks; these are 'largest observed effect' doses, not minimums.
